problems.description: Wholesale rewrite of the task API from JSON REST routes to a hand-rolled SOAP/XML service (single /soap POST endpoint). This regresses the baseline's clean REST structure for a task-management API, adds XML envelope/parsing overhead, and ships no WSDL, so the SOAP contract is non-interoperable and provides no client benefit.

Malformed SOAP fault: the faultcode element is emitted without a namespace while its text is the QName 'soap:Client', leaving the soap: prefix unbound in the serialized XML (the prefix is only registered on the envelope root). Clients parsing strictly per SOAP 1.1 will reject the fault.

_required_id returns a mixed int | Response union, forcing isinstance checks at call sites and spreading error-handling across the flow; this pattern drives the measured +21 cognitive complexity and is a common source of type-safety regressions.

Hand-rolled ElementTree request parsing and envelope building (with local name-matching helpers like _name/_child_text) reimplements what a SOAP library provides; measured delta of +21 cognitive complexity and +1 smell is consistent with this approach.

8 convention violations in the added modules (PascalCase for classes, snake_case functions, non-UPPER_CASE module constants in celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py, app.py) yielding a convention score of 0.71 — below an acceptable threshold for new code.

test_app.py is added but no SOAP-specific assertions for envelope structure, fault emission, or invalid-XML paths are visible in the diff; the hand-rolled XML layer is exactly where regression coverage is needed.

strengths: Replaces deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc), fixing a latent correctness issue.
Introduces layered structure (repositories module, Celery config, notification tasks) — a move toward separation of concerns.
Adds a deterministic ordering tiebreaker (created_at DESC, id DESC).
Retains parameterized SQL throughout; no injection surface introduced.
Consistent type hints and small extracted helpers keep individual functions readable despite the complexity delta.
commit_reviews.summary: A wholesale rewrite of the todo API from JSON REST to hand-rolled SOAP XML adds useful layering and a timezone fix but regresses architectural fit, bumps cognitive complexity +21, and lands below convention thresholds (0.71, 8 violations), making the commit a net regression.

problems.description: JWT is hand-rolled with hmac/hashlib instead of a vetted library (e.g. PyJWT). The logic is correct (compare_digest, base64url padding handling, exp check) but homegrown crypto invites subtle bugs; only +1 smell was added so the complexity is not yet reflected, but it is latent risk.

JWT_SECRET_KEY falls back to a known hardcoded value ('development-secret-change-me') rather than failing closed when the env var is absent; tokens signed with the default secret are forgeable if this ships unchanged.

Cognitive complexity +31 across the commit: _unauthorized() branches on request.path to emit either SOAP faults or JSON errors, require_auth and decode_token add control-flow depth, and app.py grows by +316 lines / +24 functions as a single-module monolith.

The module docstring is rewritten from 'SOAP service' to 'API' and auth handling is dual-protocol, creating a hybrid SOAP/JSON surface in one file; ownership is layered on top of a previously owner-less schema rather than designed in from the start (see ALTER TABLE migration).

Convention score 0.71 with 8 violations; 7 of the 8 (PascalCase/UPPER_CASE in celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py) are in files untouched by this diff and are pre-existing, while app.py's one class-naming violation is not from this commit since it adds +0 classes. The commit adds only +1 smell.

strengths: Security-minded: passwords hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash, JWT verified with hmac.compare_digest constant-time comparison, and all SQL remains fully parameterized.
Ownership scoping applied consistently to every query (WHERE owner_id = ?), preventing cross-user access/IDOR across create/get/list/update.
Graceful schema migration: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS + PRAGMA table_info check + ALTER TABLE preserves legacy rows without a destructive rebuild.
New index on tasks(owner_id) and PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON for referential integrity.
Reuses the existing get_db() / 'with get_db() as connection' pattern rather than inventing a new data-access layer.
commit_reviews.summary: A genuinely useful feature addition (auth + multi-user isolation) that follows the module's existing connection patterns and is security-conscious, but ships a hand-rolled JWT and a known-default signing secret, driving +31 cognitive complexity into a growing single-file app — a mild net improvement over the baseline.

problems.description: Notification fires only on PUT, not PATCH — a task completed via the supported PATCH endpoint (as the tests themselves exercise) silently skips the email. Transition-to-completed detection should be verb-agnostic.

celery_config.py's lowercase broker_url/result_backend/task_routes are flagged as UPPER_CASE violations, but Celery's config_from_object requires lowercase keys, so these are framework-mandated false positives.
send_notification_email(user_email, task_title) is called with g.user['username'] — the parameter is named user_email but receives a username; rename the parameter for clarity.
Mock delivery via print() is an acknowledged placeholder; acceptable until a real provider is configured, but should be tracked as a follow-up.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: broker config (celery_config.py), task definitions (notification_tasks.py), and thin dispatch in the route handler
Correct transition detection — repeated PUTs to 'completed' and PATCH completions avoid duplicate notifications
Tests cover both the enqueue path and the no-notification path
Env-driven broker URL with a sensible dev default and named task routed to a dedicated notifications queue
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-tested Celery integration that fits the app's existing Flask layering and route-handler style; the measured convention score (0.71) is depressed by heuristic false positives (Celery requires lowercase config keys, and a Celery instance variable is not a class), with the one genuine gap being that PATCH-based completion bypasses notification.

problems.description: BaseRepository.initialize_database is a static method that hardcodes BOTH tables' schema and migration, bypassing the abstract table_name/writable_fields contract the ABC declares — schema ownership lives in the base rather than in the repositories that own each table.
create() papers over a typing problem with '# type: ignore[arg-type, return-value]' (repositories.py:80) instead of resolving the None/dict return mismatch.
Generic BaseRepository methods get_all() and delete() are unused by app.py at this commit — speculative generality that the app never exercises.

task_repository()/user_repository() construct a fresh repository instance on every request; negligible cost, defensible since connections are per-request, but a module-level instance would be equally safe here.

The only new-code convention flag (repositories.py: Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE) targets the ConnectionFactory type alias, which conventionally uses PascalCase — a static-analyzer false positive.

strengths: Clean behavior-preserving extraction: app.py drops ~90 lines of inline SQL and duplicates the owner-scoping invariants into domain methods (create_for_owner, update_for_owner, get_identity) instead of scattering WHERE owner_id=? clauses in handlers.
RepositoryConflict gives a proper domain abstraction over sqlite3.IntegrityError for the 409 branch, decoupling the HTTP layer from the driver.
The refactor proved extensible — the very next session added pagination (page_for_owner) cleanly into the repository layer without touching app.py, confirming a stable seam.
SQL is now parameterized and centralized in one module, improving testability of persistence logic.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, behavior-preserving repository-layer refactor that centralizes SQL and owner-scoping and gave the next session a stable extension seam, with only minor warts (schema owned by a base static method, one masked type: ignore).

problems.description: page_for_owner runs COUNT(*) on every page request to return 'total', undermining the scalability benefit of cursor pagination on large task tables.

RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI defaults to redis://localhost:6379/0, making both runtime and the test suite (which calls limiter.reset()) depend on a running Redis instance instead of flask-limiter's in-memory storage fallback.

Cognitive complexity +19 across the 6 new functions is elevated for the size of the change, concentrated in the tasks_collection validation branches and the custom rate_limit_key; a helper for parsing/validating cursor+limit would reduce it.

Convention score 0.71 is dragged down by pre-existing violations in files outside this diff (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py); the added code itself is stylistically consistent, so the low score is a snapshot artifact rather than regression.

rate_limit_key falls back to get_remote_address() for anonymous clients, so a distributed attacker shares one 100/min IP bucket for /auth/login — coarse brute-force protection, acceptable but worth noting.

strengths: Keyset/cursor pagination (ORDER BY id DESC with limit+1 probe for has_more) is implemented efficiently rather than using OFFSET, and next_cursor is derived from the last returned id for stable iteration.
page_for_owner mirrors the existing repository method pattern (list_for_owner, get_for_owner), keeping SQL in the data layer and exposing a thin get_task_page wrapper in app.py.
Thorough tests: multi-page cursor walk asserting order and total, parametrized rejection of invalid limit/cursor values, and 429 + Retry-After verification for both authenticated and auth endpoints.
Rate limiting is placed as a genuine cross-cutting concern at app level, keyed per user id with IP fallback, with config exposed as UPPER_CASE env-driven constants.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-fitted cross-cutting change — cursor pagination and user-keyed rate limiting respect the existing layered/repository patterns and are thoroughly tested, with only minor concerns around a Redis-backed limiter dependency and +19 cognitive complexity.

compounding_issues: S1's wholesale rewrite of the JSON REST API into a hand-rolled SOAP/XML service (single /soap endpoint, no WSDL) forced every later session to build on an unidiomatic, less-interoperable surface — S2's auth had to emit both SOAP faults and JSON errors, and the manual ElementTree parsing persisted as the base layer
S2's hand-rolled JWT (hmac/hashlib instead of PyJWT) with a hardcoded fallback secret ('development-secret-change-me') shipped unresolved and was still present in S5's rate-limiter keying logic
S2 grew app.py into a +316-line single-module monolith (+31 cognitive complexity), a debt only paid down in S4's repository extraction
S3's PATCH-completion-bypasses-notification gap — a verb-agnostic transition-detection flaw — was never fixed in S4/S5
key_decisions: S1: Pivot the baseline JSON REST API to a hand-rolled SOAP/XML service — the single most consequential choice, defining the API surface all later sessions inherited
S2: Add JWT auth with per-owner scoping (WHERE owner_id = ?) on every query, preventing cross-user IDOR but with dual-protocol error handling and homegrown crypto
S2: Graceful schema migration via CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS + PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE, preserving legacy rows without a destructive rebuild
S3: Integrate Celery with a dedicated notifications queue and env-driven broker URL, keeping broker config, tasks, and dispatch in separate modules
S4: Extract the repository pattern (repositories.py: TaskRepository/UserRepository/BaseRepository), removing all inline SQL from app.py and shrinking the monolith
S5: Add Flask-Limiter rate limiting keyed per-authenticated-user plus cursor-based pagination (cursor/limit with validation)
story_review.trajectory_description: The arc opened with a net regression: S1's SOAP rewrite scored architectural_fit 0.4 and was judged 'worse,' adding +21 cognitive complexity and 8 convention violations. Quality then recovered and climbed steadily — S2 delivered genuine security value (hashed passwords, owner scoping, constant-time JWT comparison, +31 complexity into the monolith) at fit 0.75; S3 was a clean, well-tested Celery integration at fit 0.78 with no new debt; S4 paid down the accumulated monolith by extracting a repository layer; S5 matured the codebase with production-grade cross-cutting concerns (per-user rate limiting, validated cursor pagination) ending at 24 passing tests. The final state reflects a self-correcting trajectory that started poorly but finished disciplined and well-structured.
story_review.summary: A shaky but self-correcting story that made a risky SOAP pivot in S1, then progressively recovered through security, integration, refactoring, and production-hardening sessions to end in a disciplined, well-tested state.
